div.p: Many-core processors with Networks-on-Chip (NoCs) offer the scalable computational power required for complex embedded real-time (RT) applications such as autonomous driving. Migrating task between the cores forms the foundation for global and semi-partitioned RT scheduling algorithms which balance the CPU load, improve temperature distribution, and enhance fault tolerance.

In this position paper we present a concept that enables tasklevel migration in hard RT many-core systems. The concept checks the feasibility of a migration request at runtime and migrates tasks only via resources whose availability was previously tested. Our concept is not restricted to options precomputed at design time and hence increases the adaptivity and dependability of RT applications on many-core processors while ensuring predictability.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Process migration is a well-known research topic in the area of distributed computing. With the advent of multi-core processors, task migration between the cores of a single chip became possible. On multi-core processors with an uniform memory access (UMA) architecture and a symmetric multiprocessor (SMP) OS configuration, task migration merely requires modifications of the process control block (PCB) and the scheduler [1]. With an increasing number of cores, the on-chip communication fabric is typically implemented as a Network-on-Chip (NoC), which results in a non-uniform memory access (NUMA) architecture. Together with the trend to manage each core by its own OS kernel [2], adapting process migration concepts from the distributed computing domain for many-core processors becomes attractive.

Migration of tasks between the cores of a many-core processor allows to dynamically balance the CPU load and hence to improve the temperature distribution of the chip [3]. Furthermore, task migration increases the resource locality [4] and enhances fault tolerance [5]. Task migration also enables features yet unknown to embedded systems, such as adding new applications at runtime.

We foresee that many-core processors will emerge in safetycritical embedded systems with real-time (RT) constraints due to an increasing computational demand in this domain. E. g., autonomous driving requires computer vision and model-based reasoning algorithms with high computational demands. At the same time, autonomous driving applications are constraint by high fault tolerance demands and hard RT requirements. Predictability, determinism, and a-priori schedulability guarantees are of paramount importance in safety-critical embedded systems with hard RT constraints. Task migration seems to be conflicting with these goals at a first glance. Our RT task migration concept allows task-level migration only if its feasibility is guaranteed, the availability of all required resources is tested in advance, and the worst-case migration overhead is known. In order to reduce the overhead, our tasklevel migration concept performs a migration only after one instance of a task, i. e., a job, has finished its execution and before the next job of the task is started.

In contrast to existing solutions, our concept is not limited by a set of precomputed options derived at design time but performs the feasibility test online. Thus, the set of possible destinations for a migrating task is potentially larger and less memory is required to store precomputed results in general. However, not all migration requests can be fulfilled, e. g., because the destination does not have sufficient resources to handle an additional task. Therefore, we assume the requesting unit evaluates multiple destinations.

In summary, the proposed concept guarantees the application's hard deadlines on a many-core processor during a task migration by a runtime feasibility check of a migration request prior to its execution. Our task migration concept increases the possibilities for run-time management and safety mechanisms as well as global and semi-partitioned scheduling algorithms. This way, the concept increases the adaptivity and dependability of embedded systems with RT constraints.

The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Section II surveys the related work and Section III details our system model. In Section IV, we explain our RT task migration concept. In Section V, our conclusions and future work is presented.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: Task migration on many-core processors has been subject of research with focus on decreasing the migration penalty [7]. Some works also concentrate on soft RT systems where migration is often triggered by missed deadlines [6]. Only little work has been done concerning task migration in hard RT systems.

Nikolić and Petters [8] devise three agreement protocols that enable a single-threaded application to plan its future execution both temporally and spatially. An application can be executed on the subset of cores on which its instructions are present, encapsulated in a dispatcher. A task migration transfers the context between these dispatchers. The authors present an analytical and experimental evaluation of the worstcase delays of the proposed protocols that selects the next dispatcher to execute the application. In [9], Nikolić et al. extend their Limited Migrative Model approach to support inter-application communication on a separate NoC.

Hilbrich and van Kampenhout [10] evaluate methods for dynamic reconfiguration of avionic embedded systems. They focus on deterministic task migration and leverage mode changes, i. e., task-to-core mappings which are statically derived and can be switched online. Task migration is an important part of a mode change, during which no guarantees are given. The application, including its worst-case execution times (WCETs), communication latencies, and external events must be known at design time in order to define the modes.

Katre et al. [11] present a policy to guide task migration decisions on multi-core processors with temporal guarantees. The worst-case migration delays for the migrating task and the remaining tasks as well as the communication costs are investigated by an offline static timing analysis. This worstcase migration overhead is used to determine the set of feasible migrations, i. e., the tasks that can be migrated without disturbing the RT constraints of the system. The authors present a formula for the weighted migration costs, which allows to select the migration with the least costs among all feasible migrations. Different cache-line transfer policies are considered by a comparative term in the formula.
In contrast to all work presented above, our concept is not limited by static migration options precomputed at design time.

div.head: III. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: We focus on many-core processors such as Adapteva's Epiphany III [12] that integrate each core together with a local scratchpad memory into a so-called tile τ i . In conformance with the Epiphany III, we assume tiles do not contain a memory management unit (MMU). In order to execute a migrated task with a new start address, we assume tasks are compiled as position independent code (PIC) as proposed by Acquaviva et al. [6].

All tiles are connected by an NoC that represents a NUMA architecture and provides a shared memory abstraction with a global address space. We assume that the NoC provides guaranteed service (GS) communication with bounded latency and guaranteed bandwidth. This GS communication is typically achieved by reserving dedicated (virtual) channels, which are implemented by introducing temporal or priority separation of one physical channel.

In accordance with recent many-core OS research [2], each tile is managed by a local microkernel, which includes a fixedpriority preemptive scheduler. We assume a global rate monotonic priority assignment, i. e., all priority levels are valid for all local schedulers. Note that a dynamic priority assignment scheme, e. g., Earliest Deadline First (EDF), provides a simple feasibility test and would increase the utilization but is difficult to combine with the inter-task communication constraints. The OS kernel and the initial set of tasks mapped to the tile are present in the tile's local memory. As in the Epiphany III, the local memory is mapped to the same address space on every tile. Hence, OS function pointers have the same addresses on all tiles.

The application model is derived from typical hard RT systems and defined by a set of periodic tasks T. Each task is initially bound to one tile. A task t i ∈ T is specified by its state, WCET C i , period P i , and implicit relative deadline D i = P i . We assume harmonic periods, i. e., the period of each task is an integer multiple of the period of any other task. Each task t i ∈ T consist of an infinite sequence of jobs j i,j ∈ J i that are periodically activated at a i,j = kP i with k ∈ N. Note that all tile-local schedulers are synchronized, i. e., jobs of tasks with the same period located on different tiles are activated at the same time.

The state of a task includes its executable, i. e., its code and static data, and the OS-internal information, i. e., the PCB containing the task's ID, period, deadline, and priority. Note that stack, heap, and register file do not have to be migrated since we consider only task-level migration. In the following, we differentiate between the invariant state and the dynamic state. The invariant state contains all parts of the state that are not modified at runtime, e. g., the code. The dynamic state contains all variable parts, e. g., elements of the PCB. We assume that an upper bound of the size of the dynamic state of all tasks is known.

Tasks communicate with each other using a distributed message passing service (DMPS) provided by the OS. This DMPS keeps the location of a task transparent for its communication partners. In order to achieve temporal determinism, we employ the logical execution time (LET) concept [13]. In this concept, the beginning of a job's LET equals its activation a i,j and the end of a job's LET equals the next activation a i,j+1 . Communication happens logically instantaneous only at the beginning and the end of the LETs. From the implementation point of view, the DMPS has to ensure that each message is transmitted between the completion c i,j of the sending job j i,j and before the start s k,l of the receiving job j k,l that is activated at the same time or after the LET sending job, so a k,l ≥ a i,j+1 . Note that the completion of a job c i,j ≤ a i,j + R i,τi , where R i,τ is the worst-case response time (WCRT) of the task t i on tile τ i . The WCRT combines the WCET of a task with all preemptions by higher priority task and can be determined by a response time analysis [14]. The start of a job depends on the actual execution time of higher priority tasks, hence s i,j ≥ a i,j .

div.head: IV. REAL-TIME TASK MIGRATION CONCEPT
div.p: In this section, we present our migration concept. Task migration is implemented as a service at OS level. Here, we assume a feasible initial schedule for each core is given. We propose to split the migration procedure in 3 parts that are executed by: (i) the Decision Unit (DU), (ii) the Investigation Unit (IU), and (iii) the Execution Unit (EU), which will be explained in the following.

div.head: A. Decision Unit (DU)
div.p: The Decision Unit (DU) uses global monitoring and profiling information, e. g., temperature and task runtimes, respectively, in order to create new migration requests. In the current work, we assume that the DU does not issue a second migration request as long as another one is still processed. While the details of the DU are out of scope of this paper, we assume that the migration request contains the task to be migrated and a set of tiles as proposed destinations, e. g., a task t m on tile τ s should be migrated to the colder tile {τ d }.

div.head: B. Investigation Unit (IU)
div.p: The Investigation Unit (IU) receives the migration request and evaluates if the request can be executed without violating the RT constraints. The IU is implemented as a low-priority background task on every tile. On each destination tile, the local IU task checks whether the tile can receive the task t m . In the following, all steps performed by the IU are explained. If one of the steps fails, all remaining steps will be skipped and the IU will return an empty result for this destination tile.

1) The IU determines if the destination tile has enough memory to store the state of the task t m . Note that since we consider only task-level migration, the size of the task's state is known at compile time.

2) The IU checks whether the task can be scheduled by the local fixed-priority scheduler. For the application model described in the previous section, the feasibility of the new set of tasks on the destination tile can be checked by a response time analysis [14]. The resulting WCRTs allow to determine a safe upper bound of the completion times of all jobs of the tasks on the destination tile after the migration.

3) Next, the IU determines the best point in time to perform the migration. Due to harmonic periods, the hyperperiod of the task set equals the period of the task with the longest period. The IU investigates all possible migration time windows (MTWs), i. e., all intervals between the completion of a job j m,m-1 and the start of the next job j m,m of task t m in the hyperperiod of the schedule of the source tile. For the source and for the destination tile, it is checked which of the migration time windows is longer than the WCET of the EU and the WCETs of all other jobs scheduled in this MTW. If no such MTW exists, an empty result is reported to the DU. Otherwise, the longest MTW is selected, as shown in Figure 1.
Note that in contrast to a response time analysis, we search for the best-case response time of the migrating task in order to find the longest MTW to perform the task-level migration.

4) The invariant part of the migrating task's state can be copied while the task is still executed on its original tile. The variable part of the task's state has to be transferred during the runtime of the EU. For this reason, the IU asks the DMPS to test the availability of a GS channel between source and destination tile that guarantees to transmit the dynamic state of task t m during a predefined phase of the EU. Depending on the NoC, this requires to reassign the time slots [15] or to update the priority levels [16] of the virtual channels.

5) As mentioned in Section III, the DMPS needs to ensure that all messages are transmitted between the completion of the sending job and the start of the receiving job. Hence, all messages sent and received by task t m on tile τ d have to be reevaluated. For each message, the IU asks the DMPS to test if it can establish a new GS channel that fulfills the maximum latency and bandwidth requirements, assuming that the existing channels of the messages are released. The bandwidth requirements are known from the size of the message. The maximum latency is not changed for received messages, since the earliest possible start time s i,j = a i,j of a job is the same on all cores. The maximum latency of sent messages depends on the completion times of the jobs of task t m that were derived in step 2. If the test fails for one message, the DU is immediately informed about the negative result.

Note that since we consider task-level migration, the migrating task will not send any message during its migration and all messages received by the migrated task will be forwarded to its new location, so no communication is lost or blocked.

6) Due to the migration, the latency of all messages sent and received by all other tasks on the source and on the destination tile have to be reevaluated, too. Removing one task decreases the WCRTs of the remaining tasks of the source tile. Thus, the maximum latencies for transmitting messages sent by the remaining tasks of the source tile are increased and the respective channels can be kept. As explained in the previous step, the potentially earlier start times do not have to be considered. The same holds for messages received by tasks on the destination tile, whose jobs have a potentially later start time due to the additional task. However, the additional task also increases the WCRTs and delays the completion times of the jobs on the destination tile. Hence, the maximum latencies of all messages sent by the tasks of the destination tile are potentially reduced. For all these messages, the IU asks the DMPS if the respective GS channel already provides a sufficient latency guarantee. If not, the IU asks the DMPS to test whether an appropriate GS channel can be established, considering the channels tested in the previous step as reserved.

If all steps were successful, each IU returns a positive result for its tile to the DU. With its additional knowledge about the intention and severity of the migration request, the DU either waits for the results from other destination tiles or cancels the remaining IUs and triggers the EU.

div.head: C. Execution Unit (EU)
div.p: On each core, the Execution Unit (EU) is implemented as a low-priority background task that can act as sender and as receiver and is activated by the DU. Note that scheduling the EU as a high priority task would decease its WCRT. However, this would decrease the processor utilization and preempt other tasks, potentially the task to be migrated, which hinders tasklevel migration. When triggered by the DU, the EU tasks on source and destination tile are activated in their respective modes and accomplish the task migration by following steps:

1) The source EU instructs the DMPS to establish the GS channel determined in step 4 of the IU in order to transfer the invariant state of task t m . Then, the source EU copies the invariant state to the destination EU. Note that both EUs communicate directly and do not obey the LET concept.

Storing the executable in the local memory of the destination tile requires dynamic memory allocation, an uncommon feature in hard RT embedded systems. Since the task t m can continue its execution on the source tile in parallel, this step is not time critical and the unpredictability of dynamic memory allocation algorithms can be tolerated.

2) After the invariant state is present on the destination tile, both EUs wait for the completion of the last job j m,m-1 before the migration. Afterwards, the source EU notifies the DMPS to update the location of the migrating task, i. e., to release the old GS channels and establish new ones for all messages sent and received by the task t m . Messages that are currently transmitted are forwarded to the new location.
3) The source EU extracts the dynamic state of the task using features provided by the OS kernel.
4) The source EU sends the dynamic state to the destination EU via the GS channel established in step 1. Afterwards the DMPS asked to release this channel.
5) The destination EU loads the dynamic state in the kernel and adds the migrated task to the local scheduler's queue.

6) As a last step, the source EU deallocates the memory used by the migrated task on the source tile. This step is not time critical and can be executed in parallel to the execution of task t m on the destination tile.

The WCET of steps 2-5 of is critical and must not exceed the MTW. For the IU to guarantee the feasibility of the migration, the WCETs of these steps have to be known in advance. Offline static timing analysis determines the WCETs of the EU in source and destination mode. Since the size of the dynamic state is known, the duration of step 4 of the EU specifies the bandwidth and latency requirements of the GS channel tested in step 4 of the IU.
Figure 1 figuratively shows the resulting schedule of the online investigation of a migration request prior to its execution.

div.head: V. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: Our real-time migration concept increases the possibilities for run-time management and safety mechanisms, as well as global and semi-partitioned scheduling algorithms in hard RT systems.

As a next step, we plan to implement our concept in order to empirically show and analyze its functionality for realworld applications. We are especially interested in the relation between the system's utilization and the number successful migrations. Furthermore, we aim to ease the restrictive application model to support sporadic tasks and arbitrary periods. The proposed concept contributes to our long-term objective, the usage of many-core processors in embedded real-time systems.

Next, the DU activates the EUs to perform the migration. First, the EUs copy the invariant state. Once the MTW opens, the EUs copy the dynamic state and update the DMPS. Inter-task communication between tiles (t 2 → t 1 and tm → t 2 ) is depicted by dashed and dotted arrows.
